content.intro: This lesson covers Building Command-Line Applications. It sits in Module 14, Standard Library, Files, and Input/Output, and builds toward a practical Rust mental model rather than memorizing a term in isolation.
content.why_it_matters: Building Command-Line Applications matters when you work with robust interaction with external resources. Understanding the rule helps you predict compiler or runtime behavior, document assumptions, and choose a safer implementation when inputs or system conditions change.

content_blocks.title: The core idea
content_blocks.text: I/O interacts with resources outside the program and can fail for reasons the program does not control. Use Result-based error handling, portable path APIs, and explicit handling for missing or malformed input.

content_blocks.title: A reliable way to reason about it
content_blocks.text: For Building Command-Line Applications, write down the inputs, the guarantee you expect, and the boundary where that guarantee stops. Work through a minimal example first; then deliberately test one edge case. Use Path and PathBuf instead of manually joining path strings; handle I/O errors because filesystem conditions can change between checks and use.

content_blocks.run_instructions: Save as src/main.rs and run cargo run. The example uses in-memory text; replace it with read_to_string or buffered file I/O when practicing real files, and handle the returned error.
content_blocks.reset_steps: Return the sample to its original form, run the documented command again, and compare the result. If a dependency, target, runtime, database, or hardware device is required, configure that separately before treating the result as verified.

content_blocks.title: Common mistake and recovery
content_blocks.text: Do not assume Building Command-Line Applications guarantees more than it actually does. Reduce a failure to a small reproducer, read the full compiler diagnostic or error value, consult the matching official reference, and change one assumption at a time.

content_blocks.title: Toolchain and execution boundary
content_blocks.text: Course examples are static reference snippets, not executed inside CodeLeaf. Most standard-library examples can be tried in a Rust 2024 Cargo project; specialized networking, database, async, procedural-macro, embedded, and WebAssembly scenarios require the toolchain and dependencies described in their lessons.
